---
title: "Glossary"
---

Musical terms become useful when they help you hear or build something. This
glossary therefore points back to the lesson where each term first does real
work. The definitions describe how the book uses the word and recover the
central idea; the named lesson supplies the sound, code, and surrounding
argument.

### Accent

Extra weight on an event, produced by amplitude, timing, register, or timbre.
Meter becomes audible through a repeating pattern of accents. Lessons 13 and 36.

### Accidental

A sharp, flat, or natural written beside a note. Within the notation model used
here, it changes later occurrences of the same letter and octave in that voice
until the bar ends. Lesson 40.

### ADSR

The four-stage envelope of attack, decay, sustain, and release. These stages
describe how a sound's amplitude changes while and after a note is held. Lesson 7.

### Antecedent

The opening phrase in a question-and-answer pair. It usually ends with enough
instability to make a following phrase feel necessary. Lesson 34.

### Articulation

The manner in which a note begins, continues, and ends. Legato and staccato are
articulations; the pitch can stay unchanged while the gesture changes. Lesson 7.

### Bar

A fixed span of metrical time. A bar groups beats according to the time
signature and gives scoped meaning to written accidentals. Lesson 13.

### Beat

The unit used by Sonic Pi's scheduler and by a listener's pulse. Its duration in
seconds depends on the tempo. Lesson 3.

### Cadence

A harmonic ending or pause. Authentic, plagal, half, and deceptive cadences
create different degrees and kinds of closure. Lesson 29.

### Chord

Several notes treated as one harmonic event. This book begins with three-note
triads and later separates their notes into independent voices. Lesson 26.

### Chromatic

Using pitches outside the current diatonic scale, or moving in semitones. A
chromatic chord can point briefly toward another tonic. Lessons 8 and 52.

### Consonance

Relative smoothness or stability between sounding pitches. It depends on their
frequency relationship, spectrum, register, and musical setting. Lesson 5.

### Contour

The sequence of up, down, and repeated motion in a melody, with exact interval
sizes removed. Lesson 32.

### Degree

A scale position counted from its tonic. Degree numbers preserve a note's job
when a tune moves to another key. Lesson 22.

### Dissonance

Relative roughness or instability between pitches. Dissonance can be acoustic,
harmonic, or contextual, and it often supplies motion rather than error. Lesson 5.

### Dominant

Scale degree 5 and the chord built on it. The dominant is stable enough to hold
attention and unstable enough to point toward the tonic. Lesson 22.

### Drone

A sustained or repeated pitch under changing material. A drone fixes the tonal
reference, making scale-degree and modal differences easier to hear. Lesson 22.

### Duration

How much musical time an event occupies. In the event schema it is measured in
beats, independently of tempo. Lesson 12.

### Enharmonic

Two written pitch names that produce the same key on an equal-tempered
instrument, such as F-sharp and G-flat. Their spelling records harmonic function.
Lesson 10.

### Envelope

The change of amplitude or another parameter over a sound's lifetime. Envelope
shape is a large part of an instrument's identity. Lesson 7.

### Frequency

The number of pressure-wave cycles per second, measured in hertz. Doubling a
frequency raises a pitch by one octave. Lesson 4.

### Harmony

The organisation of notes sounding together and the motion from one such state
to another. Lessons 26 to 31 turn harmony into chord and voice data.

### Interval

The distance between two pitches. It carries both a diatonic number, such as
third, and a chromatic size in semitones. Lesson 18.

### Inversion

A chord arrangement in which a note other than the root occupies the bass. The
pitch classes stay the same while the chord's balance changes. Lesson 27.

### Key

A tonal environment organised around one tonic and a scale. A key supplies
defaults without restricting every pitch to its scale. Lesson 21.

### Leading tone

Scale degree 7 when it lies one semitone below the tonic. Its short upward move
to the tonic creates a strong pull. Lesson 22.

### Meter

The repeating hierarchy of strong and weak beats. A time signature describes
its grid; accents make the hierarchy audible. Lesson 13.

### Mode

A scale pattern heard in relation to its own tonal centre. Rotations of the
major-scale steps produce the seven diatonic modes. Lesson 24.

### Motive

A short musical idea that remains recognisable after controlled change. Pitch,
rhythm, contour, and articulation can each carry part of its identity. Lesson 33.

### Octave

The interval between pitches whose frequencies have a 2:1 ratio. In MIDI-style
numbering it spans twelve semitones. Lesson 9.

### Pitch class

All octave copies of one chromatic pitch treated as a class. For integer notes,
`note % 12` computes it. Lesson 8.

### Phrase

A musical unit heard as one gesture, often ending with a cadence. Phrases can
pair as question and answer. Lesson 34.

### Register

The high, middle, or low region occupied by a pitch or voice. Register affects
weight, clarity, and the space available to other parts. Lesson 9.

### Rest

A measured span in which a voice produces no new note. A rest still occupies
time in the score. Lesson 14.

### Rhythm

The pattern of event onsets and durations against a pulse. Rhythm can preserve a
melody's identity even when its pitches change. Lesson 12.

### Scale

An ordered pitch collection tied to a tonal reference. Step formulas generate
scales without storing a separate note list for each root. Lesson 21.

### Semitone

One step in the twelve-part equal-tempered octave and one integer step in Sonic
Pi pitch arithmetic. Lesson 6.

### Syncopation

An onset or continuation that shifts weight away from the meter's expected
strong positions. Lesson 15.

### Tempo

The rate of the beat, normally stated in beats per minute. Changing tempo alters
seconds per beat without changing score durations. Lesson 3.

### Timbre

The spectral and temporal character that distinguishes sounds at the same pitch
and loudness. Harmonics and envelopes both contribute. Lessons 4 and 7.

### Tonic

The pitch and chord heard as home in a key or mode. Other scale degrees are
understood through their relation to it. Lesson 22.

### Triad

A three-note chord built from a root and two stacked thirds. Major, minor,
diminished, and augmented triads use different third sizes. Lesson 26.

### Tuplet

A division that fits an unusual number of equal events into a standard time
span, such as three notes in the time normally occupied by two. Lesson 17.

### Voice leading

The motion of individual lines from one harmony to the next. Small moves and
retained common tones often make a progression sound connected. Lesson 31.

### Voicing

The chosen octaves, spacing, order, and doubling of a chord's pitches. One chord
can support many voicings. Lesson 27.
